approaches.name: Pediatric arthroscopic approach for distal-femoral epiphyseal fractures
aliases: pediatric knee arthroscopy for epiphyseal fracture
approaches.region: pediatric knee and distal femoral epiphysis
approaches.corridor: Standard anterolateral viewing and anteromedial working portals beside the patellar tendon

procedure_applications.condition: A minimally or nondisplaced epiphyseal fracture is suitable for arthroscopy-assisted assessment and fixation by an experienced pediatric knee arthroscopist

positioning.text: Position supine with a thigh support and freely mobile knee, preserving access for percutaneous fixation and fluoroscopy.

setup.text: Use only with arthroscopic expertise; prepare low-pressure irrigation, pediatric instruments, percutaneous fixation, and fluoroscopy before portal placement.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark patella, patellar-tendon borders, joint lines, femoral condyles, tibial tubercle, and anteromedial and anterolateral soft spots.

incision.text: Create approximately 5-mm anterolateral and anteromedial stab incisions at the palpated soft spots adjacent to the patellar tendon.

superficial_interval.text: Bluntly spread each portal tract and establish the medial portal under direct arthroscopic control.

deep_interval.text: Insert a blunt trocar and sleeve gently, clear hemarthrosis, inspect the epiphyseal reduction, and manipulate only under direct visualization.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, retinacular capsule, synovium, then pediatric knee articular cavity.

structures_encountered.text: Patellar tendon, fat pad, cartilage, menisci, cruciate ligaments, distal-femoral physis and epiphyseal fracture are assessed.

structures_at_risk.text: Articular cartilage, menisci, cruciates, patellar tendon, open physis, portal-adjacent nerves, and posterior neurovascular structures are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Avoid sharp intra-articular advancement and excessive pump pressure; capsular disruption can cause fluid extravasation and compartment syndrome.

retraction_hazards.text: Do not lever instruments on pediatric cartilage or the physis; add a visualized accessory portal rather than forcing trajectory.

exposure.text: Provides magnified articular-reduction assessment and survey for associated meniscal, ligament, and osteochondral injury.

limitations.text: Recommended only for minimally or nondisplaced fractures; displaced, comminuted, or unstable patterns generally require open control.

extensions.text: Add a portal under visualization or convert promptly to an open pediatric lateral or parapatellar exposure when reduction cannot be controlled.

indications.text: Consider for selected minimally or nondisplaced distal-femoral epiphyseal fractures when direct surface assessment improves reduction confidence.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid with major displacement, comminution, uncontrolled capsular leakage, infection, or unavailable pediatric arthroscopic expertise.

implant_implications.text: Plan fixation to restore epiphyseal anatomy while minimizing avoidable physeal violation and keeping implants outside cartilage.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Combine surface visualization with orthogonal and tangential imaging to confirm physis, reduction, trajectory, length, and joint containment.

closure.text: Drain irrigation, confirm soft compartments and hemostasis, and close portal skin incisions routinely.

complications.text: Complications include chondral injury, extravasation or compartment syndrome, infection, stiffness, fixation loss, and growth arrest or deformity.

bailouts.text: Stop pump inflow and convert to open exposure if extravasation progresses or stable anatomic reduction cannot be obtained.

questions.question: Which fractures are candidates?
questions.answer: Selected minimally or nondisplaced epiphyseal fractures.

questions.question: What associated injuries should be surveyed?
What pump complication is especially important?
questions.answer: Fluid extravasation and compartment syndrome when the capsule is ruptured.

approaches.name: Pediatric antegrade ESIN entry approach to the femur
approaches.corridor: Lateral trochanteric incision to paired anterolateral metaphyseal entry points distal to the greater-trochanteric physis

sources.title: ESIN Entry Points For Antegrade Nailing
Esin Entry Points For Antegrade Nailing
Elastic Stable Intramedullary Nailing for Fractures in Children - Specific Applications

procedure_applications.condition: A pediatric distal-femur or shaft pattern is selected for two-nail antegrade elastic stable intramedullary fixation

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the proximal lateral femur accessible and the entire femur imageable.

setup.text: Template nail diameter, contour, entry separation, and distance from the greater-trochanteric physis before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark greater trochanter, its physis under fluoroscopy, lesser trochanter, femoral shaft axis, and planned paired lateral entries.

incision.text: Make a 3-5 cm lateral trochanteric incision extending proximally from the planned entries to permit angled nail advancement.

superficial_interval.text: Spread fascia and lateral muscle fibers bluntly to the anterolateral femoral cortex.

deep_interval.text: Create two controlled lateral metaphyseal entries 0.5-1 cm distal to the trochanteric physis, separated at least 2 cm axially and 1 cm on the lateral plane.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia lata, lateral muscle, periosteum, then proximal femoral metaphyseal cortex.

structures_encountered.text: Fascia lata, abductor-vastus region, greater-trochanteric physis, proximal metaphysis, and medullary canal are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Greater-trochanteric physis, proximal femoral cortex, abductors, lateral femoral cutaneous branches, and femoral-neck blood supply are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Entries too close together can split the cortex; proximal or medial misplacement risks the physis or femoral neck.

retraction_hazards.text: Use blunt spreading rather than aggressive muscle stripping and protect soft tissue from rotating nail ends.

exposure.text: Provides paired antegrade elastic-nail access while avoiding the distal fracture and knee.

limitations.text: Requires adequate proximal metaphyseal space, appropriate fracture pattern, and careful growth-plate localization.

extensions.text: Lengthen the lateral incision for direct cortical control rather than creating an uncertain percutaneous entry.

indications.text: Use for selected pediatric femoral fractures treated with paired antegrade ESIN, including distal patterns where retrograde entry is unsuitable.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid when proximal anatomy cannot safely accommodate two separated entries or fracture size and stability exceed ESIN capability.

implant_implications.text: Use two appropriately contoured nails with separated entries and balanced opposing forces; avoid prominent ends that irritate lateral tissues.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm physis, entry separation, cortical integrity, canal trajectory, reduction, and nail-end position on orthogonal views.

closure.text: Confirm hemostasis and nonprominent nail ends, repair fascia as needed, then close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Complications include cortical split, physeal injury, malalignment, nail migration or irritation, infection, loss of fixation, and growth disturbance.

bailouts.text: If entry placement or cortex is unsafe, stop, enlarge exposure, revise entry strategy, or choose another fixation construct.

questions.question: Where are the usual entries?
questions.answer: On the lateral proximal femur, 0.5-1 cm distal to the greater-trochanteric physis.

questions.question: How far apart should they be?
questions.answer: At least 2 cm axially and 1 cm on the lateral plane.

questions.question: Why avoid closely spaced entries?
questions.answer: They can split the cortex during nail insertion.

approaches.name: Pediatric lateral approach to the distal femur
aliases: lateral approach for distal femoral physis
approaches.corridor: Iliotibial-band split with atraumatic anterior elevation of vastus lateralis and optional lateral arthrotomy

procedure_applications.condition: A metaphyseal, physeal, or lateral articular fracture requires direct visualization, removal of entrapped periosteum, reduction, and fixation

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the knee freely flexed and the full distal femur accessible for imaging.

setup.text: Review physeal and articular imaging, identify the tension-side block to reduction, and plan fixation that minimizes additional physeal injury.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark femoral shaft, physis under imaging, lateral condyle, joint line, patella, tibial tubercle, and fibular head.

incision.text: Begin midlateral just proximal to the physis and curve anteriorly over the lateral condyle; extend to the joint line or tibial tubercle only if arthrotomy is needed.

superficial_interval.text: Divide iliotibial band in line with its fibers and incise vastus-lateralis fascia at the posterior muscle border.

deep_interval.text: Elevate vastus lateralis atraumatically and retract anteromedially; identify and remove interposed periosteum from the displaced physeal fracture without stripping the epiphysis.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, iliotibial band, vastus-lateralis fascia, muscle-periosteal plane, then physis or optional lateral capsule.

structures_encountered.text: Iliotibial band, vastus lateralis, distal-femoral periosteum, physis, metaphyseal fragment, and lateral capsule are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Distal-femoral physis and blood supply, periosteum, lateral genicular vessels, patellar tendon, lateral meniscus, and posterior neurovascular bundle are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Avoid repeated forceful reduction and epiphyseal stripping; the injured distal-femoral physis has a high baseline risk of growth arrest.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract vastus atraumatically and protect patellar tendon and cartilage during optional arthrotomy.

exposure.text: Exposes lateral metaphyseal and physeal fractures and permits optional visualization of the lateral articular surface.

limitations.text: Complex intra-articular patterns involving the medial condyle are better seen through a parapatellar exposure.

extensions.text: Extend proximally along the lateral femoral shaft or add an anterior-third lateral capsulotomy distally to the lateral meniscus.

indications.text: Use after failed closed reduction of selected Salter-Harris II injuries and for lateral metaphyseal, physeal, or articular fractures requiring direct control.

relative_contraindications.text: Use parapatellar exposure for complex medial articular extension and avoid compromised lateral soft tissue when another safe route exists.

implant_implications.text: Restore anatomic physeal and articular alignment with the least harmful stable construct; minimize avoidable transphyseal hardware and remove it when clinically indicated.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm anatomic physeal alignment, articular congruity, implant position, and absence of unintended joint or physeal injury on orthogonal views.

closure.text: Repair capsule, vastus-lateralis fascia, and iliotibial band anatomically, then close subcutaneous tissue and skin after hemostasis.

complications.text: Complications include growth arrest, angular deformity, limb-length discrepancy, vascular injury, stiffness, infection, malreduction, and fixation failure.

bailouts.text: If medial articular reduction remains unseen, add or convert to a parapatellar exposure rather than accepting residual displacement.

questions.question: What commonly blocks reduction of a Salter-Harris II fracture?
questions.answer: Entrapped periosteum on the tension side.

questions.question: Where should the initial incision be for failed closed reduction?
questions.answer: On the side where the shaft fragment is prominent, opposite the Thurstan-Holland fragment.

questions.question: When is parapatellar exposure preferable?
questions.answer: For more complex intra-articular patterns, especially medial-condyle involvement.
